feedback: If the learner says 'adding a second bulb doesn't change the first one' (battery as constant-current source): add the second bulb live and show BOTH dim — the cell supplies a push, and the resulting current depends on the whole circuit.
If the learner conflates adding components with adding cells: place the two comparisons side by side and have them narrate each cause separately.
Affirm reasoning that keeps the two moves distinct and ties brightness to the share of push each bulb gets.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding cells and adding bulbs are opposite moves with different causes: more cells (in series) increase the push so bulbs brighten; more bulbs in series share the push so each dims. A switch simply completes or breaks the loop.
learnerActions: Starting from a steady single-bulb circuit, add a second CELL in series, facing the same way as the first, and observe the bulb brighten.
Reset, then add a BULB in series and observe each bulb dim.
Use a side-by-side compare view (two circuits shown together) to hold both moves at once.
Sort or explain: which change increases brightness and which decreases it, and WHY — 'more cells push harder; more bulbs in series share the push between more components.'
Open a switch in the loop and observe the whole loop die; explain that an open switch breaks the complete path so nothing flows.
activities.title: Hold the two opposite moves together: more cells vs more bulbs

feedback: If the learner only recites 'the current is shared' without distinguishing current from push: ask them to say what is equal everywhere (current) and what is split (the push/voltage).

For the parallel prediction: note that parallel bulbs each get (nearly) the full push of the cell and so are not dimmed the way series bulbs are — use it to test whether the reasoning transfers rather than as a recited fact.
Credit explanations that transfer the same reasoning to a buzzer's loudness or to the unscrewed-bulb case.
activities.intendedInsight: A reasoned explanation must coordinate two ideas — current is the same everywhere in a series loop, while the push (voltage) is shared between components — and this reasoning transfers to buzzers, to unscrewing a bulb, and to new configurations.
learnerActions: After a comparison, state out loud or in writing why the observed change happened.
Respond to a challenge such as 'your two bulbs are dim — why? are you sure the first isn't brighter?' and defend the answer with evidence from the circuit.

Answer probing extensions: If you unscrew the second bulb in a series pair, what happens to the first — and why? Does swapping the order (bulb-then-buzzer vs buzzer-then-bulb) change anything? Why does adding cells brighten but adding series bulbs dim?
Predict the PARALLEL case: two bulbs side by side (in parallel) compared with a single bulb, and say why.
activities.title: Explain-it-back: challenge the reason and give evidence
